title: Aurora Support Systems — Dedicated Burst beta weekly check-in
summary: Weekly burst beta check-in. Aurora reported higher-than-expected burst denials during their Monday/Tuesday batch windows (mostly cooldown + pool saturation), plus a small p95/p99 latency bump when burst traffic coincided with their interactive chat endpoint. Redwood reviewed current caps (baseline 8x H100, max burst +4 GPUs in us-east) and walked through denial reason codes seen in logs. Aurora requested (1) shorter cooldown, (2) a higher temporary burst cap for their weekly indexing run, and (3) clearer customer-visible reporting in Console (admitted vs denied, and reason breakdown). Redwood to analyze neighbor-impact indicators and propose safe tuning, with an option to schedule the batch job into a defined “burst window” to reduce thrash.
topics: Burst usage vs baseline (GPU-minutes / admitted share)
Denial reason codes: COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, POOL_SATURATED, TENANT_CAP_REACHED
Observed latency changes (p95/p99) during batch bursts
Retry behavior and 429 handling when cap is reached
Tuning requests: cooldown, max burst ratio, scheduled burst window
Console reporting and export for weekly usage review
questions: Can we shorten cooldown from 10m to ~3m without causing oscillation in the pool?
Can Aurora get a time-bounded higher burst cap (e.g., +6 GPUs for 2 hours) for weekly indexing?
Can Redwood expose denial reason breakdown and admitted/denied counts in Console per endpoint/route?
action_items: Keiko Yamamoto — Pull last 7 days of Aurora admission logs and quantify denials by reason + time-of-day; propose cooldown tuning options — Due 2025-03-20
Allison Grant — Share the current burst dashboard link set + explain the “tail amplification” panel and recommended alerts for Aurora — Due 2025-03-19
Miguel Santos — Confirm with Aurora the exact batch window(s) (day/time, duration) and whether they can pin to a consistent schedule for a burst window — Due 2025-03-19
Markus Klein — Recommend client retry/backoff guidance for 429s when TENANT_CAP_REACHED hits; send snippet/examples — Due 2025-03-21
Tom Keller — Send a couple of request IDs spanning the p99 spike window (interactive chat) so Redwood can correlate to routing/admission decisions — Due 2025-03-19
next_steps: Redwood to propose a safe increase in burst cap for Aurora’s weekly indexing (time-bounded) and/or adjust cooldown after reviewing fleet safety headroom.
Aurora to share their batch schedule and confirm whether indexing can be shifted 30–60 minutes earlier to avoid the busiest pool period.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up on 2025-03-21 to review changes and confirm denials/latency improvements.
transcript:
Meeting: Aurora Support Systems — Dedicated Burst beta weekly check-in
Recorded: 2025-03-18 17:00 UTC (10:00 PT)
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Miguel Santos (CS), Rachel Kim (CS Lead), Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Keiko Yamamoto (Infra/Guardrails), Allison Grant (Observability)
Aurora Support Systems: Priya Shah (Platform Eng Mgr), Tom Keller (SRE), Jenna Wu (ML Eng), Omar Haddad (Backend)

---

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, I think we’re recording. Hi everyone. Same agenda as last week: burst usage, denials, latency impact, any asks. Priya, do you want to kick it off?

[00:14] Priya Shah: Yep. So overall, it’s working, but we’re seeing more denials than we expected. We kind of planned for like… occasional “no,” but Monday and Tuesday we had a lot of requests not getting burst.

[00:28] Miguel Santos: Got it. When you say a lot, like a percent, or just noticeable in the job runtime?

[00:34] Tom Keller: We pulled the gateway logs. During the batch window, around 9:10 to 10:05 Pacific, we saw denial responses about, uh, 12-ish percent? It varies. And it’s clustered.

[00:50] Markus Klein: Is that the indexing job again? The one that does embeddings plus rerank?

[00:55] Jenna Wu: It’s mostly generation actually. It’s like summarization + extraction. We do embeddings too but the burst load is the gen endpoint.

[01:05] Rachel Kim: And this is on your Dedicated cluster in us-east with H100s, right? Baseline 8 GPUs.

[01:11] Priya Shah: Yes. Baseline eight. Burst cap is plus four, and I think the ratio is 1.5? I might be mixing terms.

[01:19] Keiko Yamamoto: You’re close. In the config we have baseline = 8, max burst additional = 4, so max total 12. And cooldown currently set to 10 minutes after a burst period ends.

[01:33] Omar Haddad: The cooldown thing is… I didn’t realize it was that long. That might explain some of the “clustered” pattern.

[01:41] Miguel Santos: Right, and for beta we did a conservative default. Tom, do you have the denial reason codes handy?

[01:48] Tom Keller: Yeah. I’ll read a few. We saw COOLDOWN_ACTIVE a bunch. Also POOL_SATURATED a few times. And then some TENANT_CAP_REACHED.

[02:02] Allison Grant: That matches what I saw briefly in the shared dashboard. The saturation in the shared pool had a spike around that time.

[02:09] Priya Shah: What does POOL_SATURATED actually mean in practice? Is it like there’s no GPU left in the burst pool in us-east?

[02:18] Keiko Yamamoto: Pretty much. It means the burst pool allocator is at the regional safety limit for that hardware class. It’s not “zero GPU,” it’s “we’re not allowed to allocate more without risking neighbor SLOs.”

[02:31] Priya Shah: Okay. But the COOLDOWN_ACTIVE is per-tenant? Like we used burst and then we can’t re-burst?

[02:38] Keiko Yamamoto: Yes. It’s per tenant and per pool. The goal is to avoid thrash where a single tenant repeatedly bursts in small spikes. But the tradeoff is exactly what you’re seeing: if your job pattern is like, ramp, dip, ramp, you end up tripping cooldown.

[02:56] Markus Klein: Can you describe the pattern of the batch job? Is it constant load for 45 minutes, or is it like waves?

[03:03] Jenna Wu: It’s waves. We have a queue that drains, then we do some post-processing, then it drains again. So like, 6–8 minutes hot, 2 minutes cooler, repeat.

[03:16] Rachel Kim: That’s like the worst case for cooldown if it’s set at 10 minutes.

[03:21] Tom Keller: Yep. We basically saw “admitted,” then it cools, then the next wave starts and we’re still in cooldown so it denies.

[03:31] Miguel Santos: That’s helpful. One clarifying question: are you sending the same concurrency regardless, and expecting Redwood to absorb it via burst? Or are you gating on the admit/deny signal?

[03:43] Omar Haddad: Today we’re not gating. We basically just retry. When we get denied we either see a 429 or we see like a “no burst” and it queues longer.

[03:54] Markus Klein: Small correction: the gateway can respond either immediate deny (429) or “no extra capacity, proceed at baseline” depending on route policy. For Dedicated burst, you’re mostly getting 429 when you exceed tenant cap, and baseline-only when burst is denied but baseline can still take it.

[04:13] Omar Haddad: Yeah that sounds right. It’s confusing because the client just sees slowdowns.

[04:18] Allison Grant: Do you have any user-facing latency SLOs being hit or is it just batch runtime increasing?

[04:25] Priya Shah: Both. Batch runtime is the big one. But we also saw p95 get worse on our interactive chat endpoint during that same window. It’s not catastrophic, but like noticeable.

[04:38] Tom Keller: I have numbers. Baseline p95 for /chat is ~280ms for first token. During burst window it went up to ~360, and p99 had some spikes over 900ms.

[04:55] Rachel Kim: And that endpoint shares the same Dedicated baseline GPUs as the batch job, correct?

[05:01] Jenna Wu: Yeah. We didn’t split pools. It’s the same model too.

[05:05] Keiko Yamamoto: That’s likely the main factor: within your own tenant, you’re contending. The burst pool adds capacity, but if you’re denied intermittently or oscillating, you’ll see tail effects.

[05:19] Priya Shah: So this might not be “noisy neighbor,” it’s just us.

[05:23] Keiko Yamamoto: Exactly. We still watch fleet-level neighbor indicators, but your described p95 jump aligns with internal contention.

[05:32] Miguel Santos: Allison, can you explain quickly what we’re looking at for “neighbor impact”? I want to make sure Aurora understands what we do and don’t guarantee.

[05:40] Allison Grant: Sure. We track a few things: burst pool saturation, tail amplification (p95/p99 delta for non-burst tenants sharing the same underlying pool hardware class), and a global circuit breaker. If those signals cross thresholds, we auto-reduce or disable bursting.

[05:58] Priya Shah: Right. But for our dedicated baseline, that circuit breaker doesn’t stop us from stepping on ourselves.

[06:04] Allison Grant: Correct.

[06:06] Markus Klein: One thing we can do is route your interactive traffic with higher priority within your tenant, if you’re okay with batch slowing down. But that’s more of a routing policy change.

[06:18] Priya Shah: We’d be open to that. The chat traffic is the one that pagers on.

[06:24] Miguel Santos: Let’s capture that as a potential change. Before we go there, I want to focus on your tuning asks. I heard three: shorter cooldown, higher burst cap for a window, and better reporting.

[06:37] Priya Shah: Yes.

[06:39] Tom Keller: Also, the 429 behavior. We got 429s when we hit cap. We just want to make sure we’re retrying the right way.

[06:47] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s fair. There’s a best practice: exponential backoff with jitter, and don’t do immediate fan-out retries because it makes the bucket worse.

[06:58] Omar Haddad: We probably are doing the bad thing today.

[07:01] Markus Klein: Most people do at first.

[07:04] Rachel Kim: On cooldown: Keiko, what are the levers? Can we do 3 minutes? Or is that risky for the pool?

[07:12] Keiko Yamamoto: We can tune. The risk is oscillation and starving other burst tenants if one tenant rapidly re-enters. But Aurora’s pattern is predictable and not spiky across the whole day, it’s spiky within one hour. We could do one of two approaches: reduce cooldown (say 10m to 3m), or define a “burst window” where cooldown is disabled but cap is constrained.

[07:36] Priya Shah: Burst window sounds… better? Like we can say “Monday 9-10am” and we’re allowed to burst continuously?

[07:44] Keiko Yamamoto: Conceptually yes. Implementation wise, we can approximate it with a higher token bucket refill and a smaller cooldown, plus a time-based override. We’re still working on the clean productized version.

[07:58] Miguel Santos: For beta we can do an override, but we need to be careful because we promised “no snowflakes” long term.

[08:05] Rachel Kim: But time-bounded for beta is okay if it’s in service of learning what defaults should be.

[08:10] Miguel Santos: Agreed.

[08:12] Tom Keller: On higher cap: We asked for +6 instead of +4. Would that be possible just for the indexing run? Like two hours.

[08:22] Keiko Yamamoto: Potentially. The main constraint is pool headroom. us-east H100 burst pool has been tighter in the mornings. I want to pull the last 7 days and see if we can safely allow you to 14 total (8+6) without tripping saturation.

[08:39] Allison Grant: And I can overlay that with the saturation graph so we know whether your window coincides with other tenants bursting.

[08:47] Jenna Wu: If it’s a scheduling problem, we can shift. We just need to know what times are “less bad.”

[08:54] Miguel Santos: Great. If you can shift 30–60 minutes, that might solve POOL_SATURATED without any product changes.

[09:02] Priya Shah: We can probably shift earlier. Not later. Earlier is fine.

[09:07] Omar Haddad: Monday earlier is okay, Tuesday earlier might collide with another internal pipeline. But we can check.

[09:15] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk about the perceived latency impact. You mentioned p95/p99. Did you see any change in output quality or timeouts?

[09:25] Jenna Wu: No quality changes. Timeouts: a few, but I think those are client side, like our 30-second timeout gets hit when queueing happens.

[09:35] Markus Klein: That’s consistent. If you’re doing retry storms, you can create your own queue. Also, when burst is denied but baseline is available, the request doesn’t fail, it just gets slower.

[09:48] Tom Keller: There was one more thing: we saw “admission time” be non-trivial. Like the call to the admission service, sometimes 150ms. Is that expected?

[10:00] Keiko Yamamoto: It should usually be low tens of milliseconds. 150ms might be telemetry lag or a slow path. Do you have request IDs?

[10:09] Tom Keller: I can send you a handful.

[10:12] Miguel Santos: Please do. We’ll correlate.

[10:15] Allison Grant: Also, sometimes the timestamps in logs get weird because of buffering. Not saying it’s wrong, but we should verify with tracing if you have it.

[10:25] Priya Shah: We have basic tracing, yeah.

[10:28] Miguel Santos: Okay. Switching to reporting: what do you want to see in Console that you don’t today?

[10:36] Priya Shah: Right now it’s like, we have to ask you for Grafana links. We want a simple view: “You burst X GPU-minutes this week, denied Y%, top reasons.” And ideally per endpoint because the batch and chat are different.

[10:53] Jenna Wu: Even just admitted vs denied counts would help. And the cap line. Like “you hit cap at 9:12.”

[11:01] Allison Grant: That’s aligned with what we’re building. The current beta dashboards do have it, but they’re not customer-friendly. There’s a panel called “denials by reason” and “queue depth,” but it’s more SRE-y.

[11:15] Rachel Kim: For beta we can share the dashboards plus a quick walkthrough. Longer term it lands in Console.

[11:22] Miguel Santos: Allison, can you do a 15-minute walkthrough with Tom and Priya this week?

[11:27] Allison Grant: Yes.

[11:29] Tom Keller: That’d help.

[11:31] Miguel Santos: Great.

[11:33] Markus Klein: On the 429s: do you want guidance on how to treat TENANT_CAP_REACHED vs POOL_SATURATED? Because they should be different.

[11:41] Omar Haddad: Yes please. We treat everything the same today.

[11:45] Markus Klein: Okay, so TENANT_CAP_REACHED means you’re at your configured limit; retrying immediately won’t help unless demand drops. You should back off more aggressively or shed load. POOL_SATURATED means shared pool is full; that can clear quickly but also might persist. COOLDOWN_ACTIVE is guaranteed to persist for the cooldown duration.

[12:06] Omar Haddad: We don’t actually know the cooldown duration from the client.

[12:10] Markus Klein: Today you don’t, unless you query the debug endpoint, which is internal. But we can at least provide guidance: treat COOLDOWN like a fixed “wait” of a few minutes.

[12:21] Priya Shah: It would be nice if the response told us “retry after” seconds.

[12:25] Keiko Yamamoto: That’s on our roadmap. We can add Retry-After headers, but we need to make sure it doesn’t leak too much about fleet state.

[12:35] Rachel Kim: For now, Markus can send suggested client defaults.

[12:40] Miguel Santos: I’m going to jump to the “tuning request” decisions. Keiko, can we commit to evaluating cooldown reduction, and a time-bounded cap increase?

[12:50] Keiko Yamamoto: Yes. I want to look at (a) denial breakdown, (b) pool safety cap headroom around 9–10am PT, and (c) whether we saw any non-burst tenant latency deltas. If it’s clean, we can try cooldown 3 minutes and raise cap +6 for Monday only as a first test.

[13:13] Priya Shah: Monday only is fine as a test.

[13:16] Jenna Wu: Yep.

[13:17] Tom Keller: And we can shift the batch earlier Monday if needed.

[13:22] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[13:24] (brief crosstalk)

[13:26] Rachel Kim: One more thing: you mentioned AWS SageMaker and Together last time. Are you still evaluating those for burst-like behavior? Just for context.

[13:35] Priya Shah: Not actively. SageMaker is more work for us. Together is okay but doesn’t give us the dedicated baseline + predictable isolation. The burst option is the missing piece we wanted.

[13:48] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[13:50] Allison Grant: Tom, could you share one or two exact timestamps where you saw p99 spikes? I want to check if they correlate with denial bursts or just baseline saturation.

[13:59] Tom Keller: Yeah. I wrote down 9:24 and 9:37. I’ll send request IDs from around then.

[14:05] Allison Grant: Great.

[14:07] Omar Haddad: Also, sometimes the model server logs say “key value cash eviction” — I think that’s KV cache eviction — around those times.

[14:16] Keiko Yamamoto: Yeah, KV cache pressure can happen when you push concurrency. Burst adds GPUs but if the load isn’t evenly distributed or sequence lengths are long, you can still thrash.

[14:29] Jenna Wu: Our prompts got longer recently, yeah.

[14:32] Markus Klein: That’s a big factor. Longer context means more KV memory per request.

[14:37] Priya Shah: So we might have created the problem ourselves.

[14:40] Keiko Yamamoto: Not “problem,” but it changes the shape. It’s why the system is conservative.

[14:46] Miguel Santos: Do you want to discuss prompt length changes as part of this? Or keep it scoped to burst config?

[14:52] Jenna Wu: We can keep scoped. But we can share context length distribution if that helps.

[14:57] Allison Grant: It helps. If the context jumped from like 2k to 8k, you’ll see very different batching and cache behavior.

[15:07] Tom Keller: We can export a histogram. I’ll add it.

[15:10] Miguel Santos: Awesome.

[15:12] Rachel Kim: Quick check: any concerns on audit logging / compliance as we adjust these settings in beta? I know you have internal controls.

[15:20] Priya Shah: As long as changes are logged and we know who did them, we’re fine. Our compliance folks might ask later.

[15:27] Miguel Santos: We log config changes with actor and timestamp. We can provide an export if needed.

[15:32] Priya Shah: Great.

[15:34] (pause)

[15:36] Miguel Santos: Okay, I’m going to fast-forward a bit: anything else from your side? Any surprises?

[15:42] Tom Keller: The only other thing is we saw some “admission timeout” errors once, like the call to admission timed out and then we got baseline behavior. It was rare, but it happened.

[15:55] Keiko Yamamoto: That’s actually expected fallback behavior: if admission controller is unavailable, we fail closed for burst but allow baseline to continue. We’ll check why it timed out.

[16:07] Omar Haddad: That’s good. We’d rather have baseline than total outage.

[16:11] Rachel Kim: Exactly.

[16:13] Miguel Santos: Alright. Let’s do a recap and next steps so we can give time back.

[16:18] Miguel Santos: Recap: (1) Denials are higher than expected in your batch waves because cooldown is too long for your pattern, plus some pool saturation around 9–10am. (2) You saw p95/p99 increases on interactive chat likely due to internal contention + longer prompts, not neighbor noise. (3) You want better reporting and clearer retry guidance.

[16:45] Miguel Santos: Next steps on Redwood side: Keiko will pull 7-day logs and propose cooldown tuning and a Monday test of higher cap, assuming fleet safety headroom. Allison will share dashboards and do a walkthrough. Markus will send retry/backoff guidance specifically for 429 and reason codes.

[17:05] Miguel Santos: Next steps on Aurora side: Tom will send request IDs around the p99 spikes and any admission-timeout examples, plus a context length histogram. Priya/Omar will confirm the exact batch schedule and whether it can shift earlier.

[17:22] Priya Shah: That all sounds good.

[17:24] Tom Keller: Yep.

[17:26] Jenna Wu: Works.

[17:28] Miguel Santos: Cool. Let’s keep the Friday slot? 30 minutes to review what we changed and whether denials improved.

[17:35] Priya Shah: Friday works.

[17:37] Miguel Santos: Great. Thanks everyone.

---

(End of transcript)
